import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Inscribed square problem

The *inscribed square problem* or *Toeplitz conjecture* asks whether every Jordan curve (i.e. simple
close curve in ℝ²) admits an inscribed square, i.e. a square whose vertices all lie on the curve.
There are several open and solved variants of this conjecture.

*References:*
 - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inscribed_square_problem)
 - [A Survey on the Square Peg Problem](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/274622766_A_Survey_on_the_Square_Peg_Problem)
   by *Benjamin Matschke*
 - [arxiv/2005.09193](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09193)
-/

open Topology ContDiff Manifold
open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace InscribedSquare

/-- Four points `a b c d` in the plane form a rectangle with `a` opposite to `c` iff the line
segments from `a` to `c` and from `b` to `d` have both the same length and the same midpoint, acting
as the diagonals of the rectangle. We also require the rectangle to be nondegenerate and have a
given aspect ratio `ratio : ℝ`. -/
structure IsRectangle (a b c d : ℝ²) (ratio : ℝ) : Prop where
  diagonal_midpoints_eq : a + c = b + d
  diagonal_lengths_eq : dist a c = dist b d
  a_ne_b : a ≠ b
  b_ne_c : b ≠ c
  has_ratio : (dist a b) / (dist b c) = ratio

/--
**Inscribed square problem**
Does every Jordan curve admit an inscribed square?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem inscribed_square_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (γ : Circle → ℝ²) (hγ : IsEmbedding γ),
      ∃ t₁ t₂ t₃ t₄, IsRectangle (γ t₁) (γ t₂) (γ t₃) (γ t₄) 1 := by
  sorry

/--
**Inscribed rectangle problem**
Does every Jordan curve admit inscribed rectangles of any given aspect ratio?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem inscribed_rectangle_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (γ : Circle → ℝ²) (hγ : IsEmbedding γ) (r : ℝ) (hr : r > 0),
      ∃ t₁ t₂ t₃ t₄, IsRectangle (γ t₁) (γ t₂) (γ t₃) (γ t₄) r := by
  sorry

/--
It is known that every Jordan curve admits at least one inscribed rectangle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem exists_inscribed_rectangle (γ : Circle → ℝ²) (hγ : IsEmbedding γ) :
    ∃ t₁ t₂ t₃ t₄ r, IsRectangle (γ t₁) (γ t₂) (γ t₃) (γ t₄) r := by
  sorry

/--
It is known that every *smooth* Jordan curve admits inscribed rectangles of all aspect ratios.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem exists_inscribed_rectangle_of_smooth (γ : Circle → ℝ²)
    (hγ : IsEmbedding γ) (hγ' : ContMDiff (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) ∞ γ) (r : ℝ) (hr : r > 0) :
    ∃ t₁ t₂ t₃ t₄, IsRectangle (γ t₁) (γ t₂) (γ t₃) (γ t₄) r := by
  sorry

/--
It is also known that every $C^2$ Jordan curve admits an inscribed square.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51]
theorem exists_inscribed_square_of_C2 (γ : Circle → ℝ²)
    (hγ : IsEmbedding γ) (hγ' : ContMDiff (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) 2 γ) :
    ∃ t₁ t₂ t₃ t₄, IsRectangle (γ t₁) (γ t₂) (γ t₃) (γ t₄) 1 := by
  sorry

end InscribedSquare

findings.description: The hypotheses on line 82 require a C∞ map that is a topological embedding, not a smooth embedding in the differential-topological sense. Neither `IsEmbedding γ` nor `ContMDiff (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) ∞ γ` requires an injective differential. Consequently the theorem includes singular Jordan curves beyond the regular smooth curves of the cited result. For example, `γ(z) = !₂[((z : ℂ).re)^3, ((z : ℂ).im)^3]` parametrizes an astroid. In scratch Lean I proved that it satisfies both hypotheses, but its manifold differential at `1 : Circle` is not injective. Its image has genuine cusps, so this cannot be justified merely as allowing a different parametrization of a regular smooth curve.
findings.source_evidence: Matschke, A Survey on the Square Peg Problem, p. 350, Conjecture 8 explicitly states: “Every C∞ embedding γ : S¹ → ℝ²” inscribes a rectangle of prescribed aspect ratio r > 0 (full text: https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3120610_1/component/file_3120611/content). Greene–Lobb's cited theorem is for smooth Jordan curves; its proof explicitly treats γ × γ as a smooth Lagrangian torus, requiring the curve to be a smooth embedded submanifold (https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09193, main theorem and proof). Matschke's updated account likewise states the Greene–Lobb theorem for C∞ embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0186, introduction).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the two curve hypotheses by `(hγ : Manifold.IsSmoothEmbedding (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) ∞ γ)`. Alternatively retain them and add `(himm : ∀ t, Function.Injective (mfderiv (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) γ t))`. Keep the aspect-ratio condition and conclusion unchanged.

findings.description: The C² hypothesis on line 91 has the same regularity gap: it asserts differentiability of the parametrization, without the immersion condition of a regular C² Jordan curve. The statement therefore extends the cited square-inscription result to possibly singular C² topological embeddings. The astroid `γ(z) = !₂[((z : ℂ).re)^3, ((z : ℂ).im)^3]` is a concrete witness to the enlarged hypothesis class: scratch Lean verifies `IsEmbedding γ`, the stated `ContMDiff ... 2 γ`, and failure of injectivity of its differential at `1`. Its cuspidal image is not an embedded C² submanifold. This is a missing domain restriction, not a counterexample to the square-inscription conclusion.
findings.source_evidence: Matschke's cited survey, pp. 347–348, discusses Schnirelman's result for C² curves and its smooth-isotopy proof (https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3120610_1/component/file_3120611/content). Chambers's account, linked from the cited Wikipedia article, states this C² theorem in §1 and explicitly uses that quadruples on the curve form a submanifold and that a C² isotopy has “universally bounded curvature” (https://arxiv.org/e-print/2203.02613, first theorem and following proof discussion). These concern regular embedded curves. Corroborating this convention, Cantarella–Denne–McCleary's Appendix derives the embedded C²-smooth case as a special case of finite-total-curvature curves without cusps (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1402.6174, theorem labeled `thm:FTCWC`).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the two curve hypotheses by `(hγ : Manifold.IsSmoothEmbedding (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) 2 γ)`, or add `(himm : ∀ t, Function.Injective (mfderiv (𝓡 1) (𝓡 2) γ t))` to the existing hypotheses.

reformulations.difference: The definition uses equal diagonal midpoints and lengths, together with only two explicit vertex inequalities, rather than four distinct vertices and right angles.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Put u = b − a and v = d − a. The midpoint equation gives c = b + d − a, hence a parallelogram with adjacent sides u and v. Equal diagonal lengths mean ‖u + v‖ = ‖u − v‖, which is equivalent to ⟨u,v⟩ = 0. The two inequalities ensure u and v are nonzero; all four vertices are consequently distinct. Conversely, a parallelogram with nonzero orthogonal adjacent sides satisfies these diagonal conditions. The distance quotient is exactly its side ratio, and ratio 1 gives a square. The orthogonal-side equivalence and all six pairwise inequalities were proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The existential aspect ratio `r : ℝ` is not explicitly restricted to positive values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Any witness to `IsRectangle a b c d r` has `dist a b > 0` and `dist b c > 0`, by its two inequality fields. Its `has_ratio` field therefore forces r > 0. Thus the theorem is equivalent to the version whose witnesses additionally satisfy `0 < r`; division by zero cannot occur. This equivalence, including the existential vertices on a fixed curve, was proved in Lean.

sources_consulted: Benjamin Matschke, A Survey on the Square Peg Problem, Notices AMS 61 (2014), 346–352, DOI 10.1090/noti1100; full text read at https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3120610_1/component/file_3120611/content
https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09193 and its LaTeX source at https://arxiv.org/e-print/2005.09193
https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0186 (v2) and its LaTeX source at https://arxiv.org/e-print/1001.0186
Gregory R. Chambers, On the square peg problem, arXiv:2203.02613, especially §1; https://arxiv.org/e-print/2203.02613
Jason Cantarella, Elizabeth Denne, John McCleary, Transversality in Configuration Spaces and the “Square-Peg” Problem, arXiv:1402.6174, especially the Appendix; https://arxiv.org/e-print/1402.6174
review.notes: All six substantive declarations were checked. The two unrestricted questions and Vaughan's rectangle-existence statement are faithful; no separate status mismatch was found. Reproducible tests are in /workspace/review/geometry.lean and /workspace/review/regularity.lean; both compile, and the checked equivalence and astroid lemmas have no sorryAx dependency. The astroid demonstrates the missing regularity hypothesis, not failure of an inscription conclusion. ResearchGate and the AMS endpoints were unavailable, so the cited survey was read in full from the Max Planck institutional copy. The reviewed file was not modified and matches the requested commit.

submission.summary: Replaced topological embedding plus ContMDiff hypotheses with IsSmoothEmbedding at regularities ∞ and 2, incorporating the required immersion condition. Conclusions, aspect-ratio restrictions, documentation, attributes, and other declarations are unchanged. The required compile command succeeds with only declaration-uses-sorry warnings.
